title: ‘Simply staggering’: Rapidly developing ‘super El Niño’ on track to peak in December - Carbon Brief
gist: Carbon Brief's analysis of 656 runs from 14 El Niño models projects the 2026 'super El Niño' will peak in December with a Niño3.4 anomaly around 4C, more than a degree above the 2015-16 record. Because global temperatures lag the tropical Pacific by about three months, 2027 is projected to hit ~1.74C above pre-industrial with a 96% chance of being the warmest year on record.

insights.claim: Analysis of 656 runs from 14 dynamical climate models projects the 2026 El Niño will peak with a Niño3.4 sea surface temperature anomaly of around 4C, more than a degree above the previous record set in 2015-16.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: An unprecedented El Niño implies outsized weather disruption to agriculture, commodities and energy demand into 2027.
insights.quote: models project this year’s El Niño will peak with an anomaly of around 4C. This would be more than a degree above the previous record in 2015-16.

insights.claim: Zeke Hausfather says the 2026 El Niño may end up being the strongest El Niño event in the past millennium, with nothing like it in the historical record.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Tail-risk climate scenarios priced off historical analogues may understate the 2026-27 shock.
insights.quote: We haven’t seen anything like this in the historical record and it may end up being the strongest El Niño event in the past millennium.
insights.locator: Writing on CB Connect on 5 November

insights.claim: On 18 September 2026 the daily Niño3.4 anomaly reached 3.11C, breaking the satellite-era record set in 2015.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Confirms the event is already beyond historical precedent, not just forecast to be.

insights.claim: September 2026 recorded a monthly Niño3.4 temperature anomaly of 2.84C, the highest since sea surface temperature records began in the mid-1800s.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: A record monthly anomaly signals sustained, not transient, Pacific heat release.

insights.claim: The 2026 El Niño, underway since June, has run well above any prior El Niño event at times by a full degree Celsius.

insights.so_what: The speed of development compresses the window for adaptation in weather-exposed sectors.

insights.claim: Ten of 14 climate models expect Niño3.4 temperatures to peak in December 2026, while the remaining four anticipate a November peak.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Peak timing sets when weather impacts on Asian, Pacific and South American supply chains are likely to be most acute.

insights.claim: Because global temperatures typically lag tropical Pacific warming by around three months, the 2026 El Niño will have its largest effect on global temperatures in 2027.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Heat-driven impacts (power demand, crop stress, insured losses) should be expected to concentrate in 2027 rather than 2026.

insights.claim: Carbon Brief projects the 2027 average global temperature will reach around 1.74C above pre-industrial levels, with a 96% chance that 2027 will be the warmest year on record.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: A near-certain record year is likely to intensify climate policy pressure and the political salience of 1.5C overshoot.

insights.claim: Carbon Brief's 2027 temperature projection is based on the historical relationship between year-on-year temperature changes and El Niño conditions in the preceding autumn, plus uncertainty about the rest of 2026.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Autumn El Niño state is a usable leading indicator for next-year global temperature.

insights.claim: Human greenhouse gas emissions drive almost all long-term global warming, but individual-year temperatures are strongly influenced by El Niño events.
